title: Multichain Invoker: progressive result injection, streaming backpressure, and loop defenses
creator: Avery Chen
description: Problem: As customers chain multiple tools (external APIs, internal functions, and model-invoked agents) within a single user turn, we observe subtle failures: partial or duplicated injections of tool results into the model context, unbounded recursion when tools re-enter orchestration, and degraded latency when streaming is naively paused to await tool outputs. Goal: Design and implement a multichain invoker pattern that supports streaming responses, safe progressive tool-result injection, structured output merging, and robust recursion/loop guards while remaining backward-compatible with existing function-calling contracts. This ticket covers design, prototype, tests, and a canary rollout for hosted API and Dedicated runtimes.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Streaming endpoints can emit model tokens while the invoker concurrently executes up to N tool calls without blocking token emission beyond configured SLOs.
2) Tool results are injected into the model context exactly once per invocation, with deterministic anchor points and idempotency markers visible in logs.
3) Recursion detection halts loops that exceed policy (max_depth or repeat signature) and returns a structured fallback to the caller with reason codes.
4) Existing function-calling SDKs continue to work: no breaking contract changes for synchronous function calls; new progressive injection opt-in flag available.
5) Observability: traces show per-tool latency, injection events, recursion triggers, and backpressure metrics; dashboards updated and no gaps in token billing attribution.
technical_design:
High-level approach:
- Orchestrator: introduce a per-request invoker state machine (linearized list of tool frames) that routes tool invocations through a single execution layer. Each frame has immutable id, originator token range, and an idempotency token (deterministic hash).
- Progressive injection: tool responses are buffered and injected at designated injection anchors. Anchors are either: immediate-stream (yield partial structured result as proto-chunks), end-of-turn merge (append structured block before final model prompt), or inline-rewrite (replace a placeholder token sequence). Injection mode is negotiated via an opt-in header or SDK flag.
- Streaming semantics: the runtime will maintain an ordered token emission queue. While tools run async, the model can stream prefix tokens. When an injection anchor is reached that depends on tool output, the invoker emits a structured placeholder event in-stream (type: tool-await) and resumes streaming tokens if policy allows. If policy requires blocking, the invoker stalls token emission up to a configured timeout, then emits a fallback token with structured reason.
- Idempotency and result anchoring: every tool invocation is accompanied by an idempotency token; replays are matched and deduped. Injection records are written to the request-level ledger (append-only) with per-frame SHA256 signatures to detect accidental re-injection.
- Recursion/loop guards: maintain a lightweight call graph signature (concatenated frame ids + tool id + short output hash). If a signature repeats more than threshold T within the request, the invoker stops invoking further tools and injects a structured diagnostic (loop_detected) with suggestions. Also enforce overall max_tool_calls and max_depth config per plan tier.
- Compatibility layer: expose two API surfaces: 1) legacy function-calling behavior (sync-blocking) and 2) new progressive-injection streaming mode. Compatibility shim translates legacy SDK calls to blocking invoker frames.
- Structured outputs: adoption of a minimal JSON-LD-like envelope for injected content: {"_type":"tool_output","tool":"<id>","id":"<frame>","payload":<arbitrary JSON>,"meta":{"injected_at":"<iso>","hash":"<short>"}}. The runtime will validate payload size and schema-allowlist per tool.
- Failure/fallbacks: timeouts produce a deterministic structured fallback; tool error codes map to user-visible reason codes. Network errors to downstream tools trigger circuit-breaker rules per tool id.
- Telemetry: emit events: tool_invocation.start|end|error, injection.write, injection.dedupe, recursion.detected, stream.backpressured, stream.resume. Ensure these hook into Console traces and cost attribution.
rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (canary): implement invoker state machine behind feature flag in dev cluster; enable for 1% of hosted API traffic and internal end-to-end tests for Dedicated; collect telemetry for 72h.
Phase 2 (wider canary): 10% traffic with opt-in SDK flag; add more aggressive chaos tests for tool latencies and random tool replays.
Phase 3 (default opt-in): expose new progressive injection mode behind account-level toggle; update docs and SDK samples.
Phase 4 (GA): flip default for newly-created projects; provide migration guide for legacy callers.
Rollback: feature flag off and ensure ledger-dedup map is read-only to avoid partial state changes.
Metrics to monitor: injection success rate, duplication rate, recursion triggers per 1k requests, 95th token latency delta, tool error rate, and user-visible fallbacks.
risks: 1) Complexity in streaming semantics may cause increased tail latency when many concurrent tool calls are inflight. Mitigation: conservative defaults and adaptive backpressure policies.
2) Mis-specified structured payloads could leak PII if schema allowlist is too permissive. Mitigation: tool-level schema enforcement and KMS tagging for sensitive fields.
3) Behavioral divergence between legacy blocking semantics and progressive mode might break client assumptions. Mitigation: clear doc, SDK helpers, and deprecation windows.
4) Incorrect deduping could hide legitimate repeated tool runs. Mitigation: include human-readable audit traces and an opt-out for strict re-execution when safe.
5) Scale: maintaining per-request ledger increases memory pressure. Mitigation: bounded ledger size, eviction after response completion, and spill-to-blob for large payloads.
test_plan: Unit: state machine transitions, idempotency token generation, signature collision tests.
Integration: synthetic chains of 1..20 tool calls with varied latencies; verify injection count and order.
E2E: SDK flows exercising legacy and progressive injection modes across hosted and Dedicated backends.
Chaos: randomized tool failures, delayed responses, and simulated recursive tool behavior to assert loop guards trigger correctly.
Performance: throughput and token-latency benching with and without progressive injection at 95/99 percentiles.
